classification.difficultyReason: Derive the directed triple-angle expression, factor the resulting cubic and use angle ranges to identify the desired root, then interpret the remaining positive root through complementary angles.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that $\tan\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$ is a root of the equation

$$t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$$

by considering the expansion of $\tan(3\theta)$.

answer.worked:
Let $t=\tan\theta$. Using the sum and double-angle formulas,

$$\begin{align*}\tan3\theta&=\frac{\tan2\theta+\tan\theta}{1-\tan2\theta\tan\theta}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{\frac{2t}{1-t^2}+t}{1-\frac{2t^2}{1-t^2}}\\\tan3\theta&=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}.\end{align*}$$

Set $\theta=\frac{\pi}{12}$, so $\tan3\theta=\tan(\frac{\pi}{4})=1$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}&=1\\3t-t^3&=1-3t^2\\t^3-3t^2-3t+1&=0.\end{align*}$$

Thus $\tan(\frac{\pi}{12})$ is a root.

answer.short:
$\tan\left(\dfrac\pi{12}\right)=2-\sqrt3$.

Factor the cubic as $(t+1)(t^2-4t+1)$ and select the root in $(0,1)$.
answer.worked:
Let $P(t)=t^3-3t^2-3t+1$.

$$\begin{align*}P(-1)&=-1-3+3+1\\P(-1)&=0\\P(t)&=(t+1)(t^2-4t+1).\end{align*}$$

By part (a), $t=\tan(\frac{\pi}{12})$ is a root. Since $0<\tan(\frac{\pi}{12})<1$, the root $-1$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}t^2-4t+1&=0\\t&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4}}2\\t&=2\pm\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$

Only $2-\sqrt3$ lies in $(0,1)$, so $\tan(\frac{\pi}{12})=2-\sqrt3$.
